text: One single page, telling one clear story at a glance — that's genuinely what a Power BI dashboard is, and it's the very last piece of this entire chapter, built entirely inside the service itself.

Chapter Eight's whole discipline — headline number first, with everything else supporting it — was preparing you directly for exactly this moment. A dashboard is that same discipline, expressed as an actual, real Power BI object with its own name and its own specific rules.

Individual tiles get pinned onto a dashboard from somewhere else entirely — most often a report page, but also from another dashboard, from Excel, or from a Q and A result. And because of that layered relationship, one single dashboard can pull tiles from more than one report, and even more than one semantic model, into a single consolidated view that no individual report page could ever manage on its own.

Dashboards and reports differ in ways that genuinely matter in daily use. A dashboard is exactly one page, while a report can hold many. A dashboard can't be filtered or sliced at all, while a report supports that extensively. A dashboard is never available inside Desktop at all, only in the service. But dashboards do support one thing reports don't: real alerts, configured directly on individual tiles.

That genuinely closes out Chapter Nine. Chapter Ten, Refresh and Gateways, picks up the thread this whole chapter kept mentioning only in passing: exactly how these published semantic models actually stay current once your real, on-premises data keeps changing underneath them.
